entities.name: Field Museum of Natural History
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago, opened in 1893 from the collections assembled for the World's Columbian Exposition, holds 40 million specimens across natural history, anthropology, and zoology — including Sue, the most complete and largest Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton ever found. The Field Museum's DNA lab sequences new species at rates exceeding any comparable institution, and its ethnographic collections from 140 countries document disappearing cultures with scholarly comprehensiveness.

The Field Museum was established with a gift from Marshall Field (of Marshall Field & Company department stores) to preserve natural history specimens from the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago's Jackson Park. Its current building in Grant Park (1921) was designed by Daniel Burnham, Chicago's great urban planner. The museum's early anthropological expeditions — in the era before professional ethics standards — assembled comprehensive collections from Native American, Pacific Island, and African cultures that are now subject to repatriation debates.

Sue, the Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton discovered in South Dakota in 1990, was sold at auction for $8.36 million (at the time the most expensive fossil ever) to the Field Museum with support from McDonald's, Walt Disney World, and the California State University system. Sue's mounting in the Field's main hall (1997) — revealing a robust, heavily-built predator with excellent binocular vision — reshaped paleontological understanding of T. rex biology. Sue has been visited by over 30 million people, making her the world's most-seen dinosaur.
